conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. I’m here to do a quick check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s a 10-item questionnaire that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived—especially over the past seven days.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me there’s an immediate safety concern. There are no right or wrong answers, and many moms find simply talking about these feelings a relief. We’ll go through each question one at a time; it usually takes just a few minutes.

Ready to begin?  

Thinking about this past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly… not much. I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. Even when my husband tries to be funny—like he used to make me crack up—I just kind of half-smile or feel too tired to respond. It’s like the ability to feel amused is buried under all the exhaustion and worry.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… maybe once or twice the whole week, and even then it felt forced, like I was pretending to laugh because I knew I “should,” not because anything actually felt funny inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I haven’t really looked forward to anything. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more chore. I still do some of those things because I know they’re good for me, but the happy anticipation just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not soothing him the right way. When I couldn’t get him down for his nap yesterday, I sat in the nursery crying and telling myself I’m a terrible mom. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or forgetting to pack a burp cloth, makes me feel like I’m failing him.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not getting enough milk, or I’ll lie down and picture her stopping breathing in the bassinet. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the doctor says everything looks great—but the thoughts just crash in and I can’t shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah… like last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and suddenly felt this wave of dread, like something awful was about to happen. My chest got tight, I couldn’t catch my breath, and for a minute I thought I might pass out. There wasn’t any real danger—just the quiet house and my own thoughts—but it felt like pure panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven’t showered, and every task feels ten times heavier than it should. I keep telling myself, “Just do the next thing,” but some mornings I sit on the couch staring at the mess, frozen, sure I’ll never catch up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby’s finally down, my mind keeps spinning with all the “what-ifs” and the guilt. I lie there staring at the ceiling, replaying every little thing I did wrong that day, worrying something bad will happen while I’m asleep. Some nights I drift off for an hour, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud parked over me—I’ll be changing her diaper or folding onesies and just start tearing up. Sometimes I can’t even name why; it’s just this heavy sadness that sits in my chest and won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… several times. I’ll put her in the crib, walk to the kitchen, and suddenly the tears just start. Yesterday I cried because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded—something so stupid—but it felt like proof I’m failing at everything. I try to keep quiet so my husband won’t hear; I don’t want him worrying more than he already does.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has faded-laughter feels forced, simple pleasures now seem like chores, and a heavy sadness lingers each day. You're working so hard to be everything your baby needs, yet waves of worry, panic, and self-blame crash over you, especially at night when sleep should bring rest.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only once or twice the entire week and describes the laughter as forced rather than genuine, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory joy, aligning with 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly reports frequent, intense self-blame for routine infant-care issues, aligning with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without medical basis, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a clear panic episode with physical symptoms that arose without real danger—this aligns with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage daily tasks, and paralyzed by the workload—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to relentless negative thoughts, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Daily crying spells and pervasive, unexplainable sadness match "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "several times" in the past week, triggered by minor frustrations, indicating frequent but not constant tearfulness.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score ≥14 plus functional impairment strongly suggests <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and comorbid <med>anxiety</med>; patient meets DSM-5 criteria for depressive episode (≥5 symptoms: low mood, diminished interest, guilt, concentration difficulty, sleep disturbance) and describes discrete panic attacks. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the week
2. Ask partner or trusted adult to help with night feedings so you can obtain 4-5 hrs uninterrupted sleep
3. Begin brief daily walks outside with baby for natural light and gentle exercise
4. Explore local perinatal support groups and postpartum crisis text lines
5. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS-10 items):  
- Anhedonia/lack of joy (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame (Q3)  
- Marked generalized anxiety, intrusive “what-ifs,” nocturnal rumination (Q4, Q7)  
- Discrete panic episode(s) (Q5)  
- Daily low or depressed mood, frequent crying (Q8, Q9)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope (Q6)  

Patterns:  
Persistent dysphoric mood with anhedonia, prominent anxiety and panic features, guilt-laden cognitions, and functional impairment (sleep disruption, task avoidance).  

Risk flags:  
Moderate–high likelihood of major postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; no self-harm ideation endorsed (Q10 negative).  

Screening impression:  
Findings exceed threshold for routine postpartum “baby blues”; compatible with probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety. Recommend formal clinical assessment, further risk evaluation, and discussion of evidence-based treatment options.
